newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Police arrest three more after Timor market fire.
newsitem.headline: Police arrest three more after Timor market fire.

text.p: Indonesian police in troubled East Timor have arrested three more people over a fire that swept the largest market in the territory's capital Dili last week, the official Antara news agency reported on Thursday.

"After further police investigation, the number of people accused of burning the Mercado Lama (Old Mercado) market increased from six to nine. They are being intensively investigated," East Timor police chief Colonel Jusuf Muharam was quoted as saying.

Antara said at least 30 kiosks were burnt down in the market, but other media reports have said around half of the market's 320 stalls were burned in the fire, which started on Saturday night and lasted for more than two hours.

Muharam said police were questioning 15 other people about the fire, and that the suspects had admitted they had been ordered by a leader of the separatist movement from Baucau, 130 km (81 miles) east of Dili, named David Alex, to burn the market.
"They (suspects) have been ordered by David Alex to disturb the security in Dili by burning markets and attacking military headquarters," he said.

At least 34 people died as a result of attacks by rebels seeking to disrupt the May 29 general elections, in which Indonesia's ruling Golkar party swept 74 percent of the vote nationwide, police have said.
Indonesian security forces in Timor have since captured 120 members of the guerrilla movement opposing Jakarta's rule in the territory.
Indonesia occupied the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has expressed concern at reports of recent violence in East Timor and called on all parties to exercise restraint.
Annan is scheduled to hold the next in a long series of meetings on East Timor with the foreign ministers of Indonesia and Portugal on June 19 and 20 in New York.
The meetings, to try to find an internationally acceptable solution to the issue, were initiated in 1983 by then Secretary-General Javier Perez de Cuellar.
